name: Cartagena
title: Cartagena Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging | Tankers & LNG Carriers
description: Ship thickness measurement at Cartagena and Escombreras for crude and product tankers, LNG carriers, bulkers and cruise ships: UTM of hull, tanks and piping.
h1: UTM at Cartagena and Escombreras: Hull Gauging for Tankers and Gas Carriers
intro: Cartagena is a naval city with an energy port next door: the Escombreras basin serves a refinery, a gas regasification terminal and a steady line of tankers, while the main harbour handles cruise ships, bulk cargo and the naval yard's activity. Many calls are shaped by terminal permits. Our ultrasonic thickness team travels from India to the vessel, with port access arranged by the ship's agent, and prepares a scope that suits tanker, gas carrier, bulker or passenger ship.

highlights.h: Escombreras tanker and gas carrier calls
highlights.p: Crude, product and gas carriers discharge at the Escombreras energy basin under strict permit rules. Hull, deck, ballast tank and piping readings can be planned within those rules, with the scope agreed before the ship arrives.

highlights.h: ESP tank programmes before the survey
highlights.p: Tankers approaching a renewal survey need ballast tank and cargo tank readings that show where substantial corrosion is starting. We read the plating and structure so the superintendent can plan steel renewal before the docking yard is booked.

highlights.h: A choice of docking yards nearby
highlights.p: Cartagena sits between Valencia and the Strait, with yards in Spain, Gibraltar and North Africa within reach. Measured steel data supports a fair comparison of quotations and a better docking decision.

port.h: The port of Cartagena: a natural harbour and the Escombreras energy basin
p: Cartagena owns one of the best natural harbours on the Spanish Mediterranean, a deep bay protected by high headlands and entered through a narrow mouth. The Autoridad Portuaria de Cartagena manages two quite different areas. The city harbour, below the old town, has the cruise berths, the passenger terminal and general cargo quays, with the naval base and the Navantia yard occupying a large share of the shoreline. Round the headland to the west lies the Escombreras basin, an industrial port with its own approach, deep-water berths and a skyline of tanks and process plant.

Escombreras is the reason Cartagena matters to tanker owners. A refinery and petrochemical complex receives crude and ships out products, and a gas terminal receives LNG carriers, so the berths see a continuous flow of tankers of different sizes. Chemical, LPG and bunker vessels also use the basin. Bulk cargoes such as grain, fertiliser and minerals use quays elsewhere in the port, and ro-ro and container traffic is smaller but regular. The harbour mouth is wide enough for large ships and the pilots board outside, although strong southerly winds can slow operations and keep ships at anchor.

The pattern of work follows the energy cycle. Tankers arrive on cargo programmes, discharge or load, and leave, with stays of one to two days being typical, and the terminals insist on safety procedures that determine who can board and what equipment is allowed. Cruise calls reach a peak in spring and autumn. Tides are small, so depth at the berth hardly changes, and long stays are mostly for ships waiting for cargo or an operational slot. The large anchorage off the port is used by tankers and bulkers for orders, supplies and crew changes, so gauging at anchor comes up regularly on tanker enquiries.

facilities.h: Where gauging takes place in Cartagena and Escombreras
p: Most tanker work happens at the Escombreras berths, where the ship is bound by terminal permit-to-work rules and the cargo programme. Spaces that are inert or gas-free can be gauged once the ship's enclosed-space entry system is in place, and we tailor the scope to what the chief officer can prepare during discharge. Bulk and general cargo ships in the main harbour offer more relaxed access, with holds, decks and ballast tanks readable once the cargo operation has paused.

The naval yard in the city is a specialist facility geared to its own customers, and merchant ships needing drydocking normally go to yards elsewhere in the western Mediterranean. Cartagena has repair firms for afloat work, including piping, tank cleaning and steel renewal in some cases, and these can be coordinated with gauging so the findings feed straight into the repair list. When a deep docking is needed, the choice is usually between yards in Spain, Gibraltar and across the Strait, and thickness readings taken in Cartagena make the comparison more precise. Anchorage work is possible for short jobs, subject to sea state and launch availability.
list: Escombreras tanker and gas berths — hull, deck, ballast tank and piping readings under terminal permit-to-work rules during discharge
Bulk and general cargo quays in the main harbour — hold frame, hatch coaming and deck gauging after discharge
Cruise and passenger berths — voids, sea-water lines and scrubber piping on turnaround days
Port repair firms for afloat work — gauging combined with piping and plating repairs so steel renewal is planned in one stop
Cartagena anchorage — short sampling jobs on tankers and bulkers waiting for orders, subject to weather and launch access
Docking yards elsewhere in the western Mediterranean — gauging started here continues alongside the docking survey

context.h: Port state control, ESP rules and the energy trades
p: Port state control at Cartagena is under the Paris MoU, carried out by the Capitanía Marítima of Cartagena under the Dirección General de la Marina Mercante. Tankers and gas carriers are subject to extra scrutiny because of their cargo, and inspectors are quick to examine structural condition and corrosion of ballast tanks and deck piping. For ships under the Enhanced Survey Programme, thickness records are central to how class and the owner track substantial corrosion between surveys.

The energy character of the port brings its own pressures. Tanker owners need to keep ships in demand with refiners and charterers, many of whom ask for a recent thickness picture or a condition assessment before taking a ship on. EU rules add detail: the Ship Recycling Regulation requires an Inventory of Hazardous Materials, EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime affect voyages calling here, and shore-side projects around Escombreras keep energy flows changing. Older product tankers and gas carriers trading in this area benefit from having a readings history, and pitting or grooving in ballast tanks is easier to manage when it is measured early.

jobs.p: Cartagena work divides between tanker and gas carrier surveys at the Escombreras berths and lighter work on cruise, bulk and general cargo ships in the main harbour. The terminal's safety rules and the ship's cargo programme set the limits, and we agree spaces, access and the report format with the superintendent before the team travels. Examples of work that suits this port:
list: Ballast tank and deck gauging on a product tanker discharging at Escombreras, ahead of a renewal survey and a steel estimate.
Hull, deck and piping readings on an LNG carrier alongside, within the terminal's permit rules and without touching cargo containment.
Condition gauging for a charterer or buyer, giving a measured view of ballast tanks, deck and main structure.
Hold frame and hatch coaming readings on a bulk carrier after discharge in the main harbour.
Scrubber overboard pipe and sea chest gauging on a cruise ship or tanker, compared with readings from an earlier visit.

logistics: The team normally flies to Murcia-Corvera or Alicante-Elche airport, the latter having wider European and Gulf connections, and continues by road to Cartagena. Valencia is another option with a long road transfer. Port and terminal passes for Escombreras are arranged by the ship's agent, who also books a launch for anchorage work. Schengen visas are required, so please provide expected dates early; we confirm mobilisation once visas are issued, because tanker calls can move with cargo programmes.

faqs.q: Can a tanker be gauged while discharging at Escombreras?
faqs.a: Yes, within the terminal's rules. Ballast tanks, voids, cofferdams, deck lines and the shell above the waterline can be read while cargo moves, provided spaces are gas-free or inerted as the ship's procedure requires and the terminal gives permission. Cargo tanks need more planning, so those are best handled when the ship is out of service.

faqs.q: Do you work on LNG carriers in Cartagena?
faqs.a: We take ultrasonic readings on hull structure, ballast tanks, decks and piping, and we do not inspect cargo containment systems. The terminal's access rules apply and the scope is set in advance with the ship manager, so that the team boards with a clear list of spaces and the gauging fits the discharge programme.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Cartagena for merchant ships?
faqs.a: The naval yard works mainly for its own customers, so owners generally dock merchant ships elsewhere in the western Mediterranean, in Spain, Gibraltar or North Africa. Gauging in Cartagena gives the superintendent a measured basis for steel estimates, so quotations from different yards can be compared on the same figures.

faqs.q: Can readings be taken at the anchorage?
faqs.a: Short jobs are possible when a launch is arranged and the sea state allows it. Tankers and bulkers waiting for orders can give several hours, though the berth call can come at short notice. A narrow list of tanks and lines works best, with the rest left to a berth stop when the timing is more certain.

faqs.q: How is the report used for a condition assessment?
faqs.a: The readings are laid out to follow the usual thickness report structure and show where wastage sits relative to the allowable diminution. A charterer or buyer can read it as a record of condition. Whether it counts for credit to a class survey is a separate question, covered in the class section on this page.
